title: Uno, 8-bit timer, prescaler 1024. How often does it overflow (Hz, integer)? What does this print?
explain: The timer tick is 16 MHz / 1024 = 15625 Hz. An 8-bit timer counts 256 steps (0 to 255) before overflow. 15625 / 256 = 61 Hz. 8-bit means 2^8 = 256 values. It does not mean divide by 8.

title: Uno, Timer1, prescaler 64, you want a 20 ms period (servo). What value goes into OCR1A (TOP)? What does this print?
explain: One tick is 4 µs (64 / 16 MHz). 20 ms / 4 µs = 5000 steps. The counter starts at 0, so it counts 0 to 4999. TOP is steps - 1 = 4999. Check by multiplying back: 5000 x 4 µs = 20 ms.

title: 16 MHz clock, prescaler 64. How many steps are 1 ms? What does this print?
explain: Tick = 64 / 16 MHz = 4 µs. 1 ms = 1000 µs, so 1000 / 4 = 250 steps. A common slip: 1 ms is 1000 µs, not 10000 µs, so 2500 is wrong. Always check by multiplying back: 250 x 4 µs = 1 ms.

title: Uno sweeper works by luck. Set the step to 2 and the servo jumps. Tap the bug.
explain: step is unsigned, so -1 becomes 65535. angle += 65535 wraps and acts like -1, but only by luck. With step -2 and angle 1, the result is 65535, which is >= 180, so the servo jumps. Also angle <= 0 can only mean angle == 0. Use a signed type (int16_t).

title: Servo on Uno. Your code calls servo.write(90) every 15 ms. The servo needs a pulse every 20 ms. What does servo.write() do?
options: It only stores the new pulse width. Timer1 interrupts send the pulse every 20 ms, using the last stored value.
It sends one pulse at once and waits 20 ms.
It starts a new 20 ms timer each time it is called.
It blocks until the next 20 ms slot, so calling it every 15 ms is a bug.
explain: servo.write() only saves a number in the library. A Timer1 interrupt makes the pulse every 20 ms with the newest number. So calling write more often is safe: extra values are overwritten. No sync is needed. Some steps are just never sent as a pulse.

title: Your USB source has about 0.5 Ω internal resistance. The servo draws 2 A. What is the voltage at the Arduino 5V pin? What does this print?
explain: Every source has internal resistance. It works like a small resistor in series. U = I x R: 2 A x 0.5 Ω = 1 V is lost inside the source. The pin gets 5 - 1 = 4 V. Big current spikes (a servo starting) can reset the MCU. Use a separate supply for the servo.

title: Same 16 bits, two readings (GCC, two's complement). What does this print?
explain: The bits are the same: 1111 1111 1111 1111. Unsigned reads all 16 bits as a size: 65535. Signed uses the top bit as the sign (two's complement): -1. Timer registers like TCNT1 are unsigned 16-bit: 0 to 65535, not 32767.

title: STM32 timer clock is 36 MHz. You want a 1 MHz tick (1 µs). Which value goes into PSC? What does this print?
explain: The hardware divides by PSC + 1. For divide by 36, write 35. Writing 36 gives 37 and a 0.973 MHz tick, so all timings are about 3% off. Same family as TOP = steps - 1: a counter that starts at 0 needs a minus one.

title: Why does the Servo library on Uno not use Timer0, although it is a normal 8-bit timer?
options: The Arduino core already uses Timer0 for millis(), delay() and micros(). Changing it would break them, and your millis() Sweeper.
Timer0 is the CPU timer. The CPU cannot share it.
explain: Timer0 is a normal timer, not a CPU timer. The CPU runs straight from the 16 MHz clock. But the Arduino core owns Timer0 for millis(), delay() and micros(). A Servo change would make time wrong. Timer2 is only 8-bit (256 steps), too small for 5000 steps. Timer1 is 16-bit, so Servo uses it.

title: Timer math: 5 steps, no slips
bullets: Write the inputs first: f_clk, prescaler, time wanted. Many slips are a wrong input (64 MHz vs 16 MHz).
tick = prescaler / f_clk. Example: 64 / 16 MHz = 4 µs.
steps = time / tick. Example: 20 ms / 4 µs = 5000.
TOP = steps - 1 (the counter starts at 0). STM32 PSC works the same: write divider - 1.
Check by multiplying back: 5000 x 4 µs = 20 ms. 8-bit = 256 steps, 16-bit = 65536. Big steps need a 16-bit timer.
